ts3_darby.topic: John Nelson Darby, the Plymouth Brethren, Powerscourt and the rapture-origin dispute

claims.text: Darby born 18 November 1800 Westminster, died 29 April 1882 Bournemouth; Westminster School and Trinity College Dublin (Classical Gold Medallist 1819); joined an inn of court but judged law in conflict with his faith

Ordained deacon of the Church of Ireland 1825, priest 1826; curate at Delgany, Co. Wicklow; resigned the curacy in protest when Archbishop William Magee required converts to swear allegiance to George IV; believed to have left the Church of Ireland around 1831 (year uncertain)

Around 1827-28 Darby joined a Dublin meeting with Anthony Norris Groves and J. G. Bellett to 'break bread'; by 1832 a distinct assembly; 1848 split into Open and Exclusive Brethren, with B. W. Newton a party to the dispute
Around 1827-28, after a riding accident, Darby came to believe the 'kingdom' of Isaiah and the Old Testament was entirely different from the Christian church

Powerscourt conferences held annually 1831-33, organised by Lady Powerscourt (Theodosia Wingfield); Darby publicly set out his ecclesiological and eschatological views there, including the pre-tribulation rapture (Dictionary of Premillennial Theology p. 82)
Notebooks of the 1831 Powerscourt conference survive; James Fazio argues they show Darby resisting pre-tribulational views at the 1831 conference; others dispute any Irving/MacDonald influence
Darby translated the Bible into German (Elberfelder), French (Pau) and English (posthumous New Translation)

Jerusalem Quarterly (Kuttab 2018) names among Christian Zionism's 'luminaries' 'Reverend John Darby and Cyrus Scofield'; dispensationalist views on the Jews placed dispensationalists 'at the forefront of Christian Zionism'
Margaret MacDonald (1815-1840), Port Glasgow; her c.1830 utterances first published 1840; 1861 version omitted two passages with a posttribulation view

Samuel Prideaux Tregelles alleged Darby's rapture concept came from a charismatic utterance in Edward Irving's church; Dave MacPherson (The Incredible Coverup; The Unbelievable Pre-Trib Origin, 1973) argued the source was MacDonald's 1830 vision

Counter-arguments: Darby and Newton investigated the 1830 manifestations and judged them demonic; Darby had written pre-tribulation views by January 1827 (Bray 1992); MacDonald's text reads as posttribulational; Walvoord calls the link untenable

Strand (Andrews University, non-dispensationalist reviewer, 1975): 'the case for the "unbelievable pre-trib origin" falls apart'; 'It is impossible to prove that Darby adopted' the view from MacDonald; her words do not show a secret rapture; Baxter attributes the view to Irving, 'not Margaret Macdonald'

Thomas Ice (Pre-Trib Research Center) argues Darby held pretribulationism by December 1826 or January 1827, citing Darby's 1879 letter: 'What set me free in 1827 is still the theme on which my soul dwells'; says MacDonald's text 'does not come close to even teaching a pre-trib rapture'

ts3_system.topic: What Darby's dispensationalism teaches about Israel and the church

claims.text: Darby, Geneva 1840 lectures titled The Hopes of the Church of God in connection with the destiny of the Jews and the nations: 'The church is in relationship with the Father, and the Jews with Jehovah'; church's calling is 'participation in a coming heavenly glory'

Darby Lecture 10: 'though the people of Israel will be restored in their land, there will only be a remnant saved'; 'those who rejected the Christ will be subjected to the Antichrist'; 'Two thirds of the inhabitants will be cut off in the country of Israel itself after their return'; 'The gospel does not occupy itself with the earthly blessings of the Jews'

Weber: dispensationalism held 'God had two completely different plans operating in history', one for an earthly people Israel, one for a heavenly people the church; God 'suspended the prophetic timetable at the end of Daniel's sixty-ninth week'

Weber: 'secret, any-moment, pre-tribulational Rapture'; 'Once the heavenly people of God have been raptured, Darby believed, the divine script can be played out to the end'; Antichrist rises; Daniel's seventieth week concludes

Weber: earlier premillennialists placed the rapture at the end of the tribulation; dispensationalists separated rapture from Second Coming; A. A. Hodge called it 'an unscriptural and unprofitable theory'
Weber: premillennialists read 'signs of the times', including 'the rise of Zionism'

ts3_niagara.topic: Darby in America, Brookes, Niagara, the 1878 prophetic conference, Moody, Gaebelein

claims.text: Darby made at least five journeys to North America between 1862 and 1877 (Wikipedia, citing the index of his correspondents); rd1 s05 says six; mostly New England, Ontario and the Great Lakes

'America did not embrace Darby's ecclesiology as it did his eschatology' (Wikipedia, unsourced); Stunt: dispensationalist eschatology was 'the one aspect of his teaching that really caught on in North America'; Akenson acknowledges Sandeen's pioneer work

Niagara origins: 1868 informal meeting in New York of men linked to Waymarks in the Wilderness; 1875 near Chicago (West, Brookes, Erdman, Parsons); July 1876 Swampscott, named Believers' Meeting for Bible Study; Niagara-on-the-Lake 1883-1897; Brookes drew up a 14-point statement in 1878, officially adopted 1890

Wikipedia: founded 1875; Brookes the driving force; creed of 14 articles does not explicitly affirm dispensationalism but refers to the millennium and the restoration of Israel; met annually to 1897 except 1884

Niagara Creed Article XIV: world 'will not be converted during the present dispensation' but 'is fast ripening for judgment'; Christ 'will come in person to introduce the millennial age, when Israel shall be restored to their own land'

Weber: Brookes 'presided for more than 20 years and was primarily responsible for drawing up the 1878 "Niagara Creed"'; met two weeks each summer; 'the First American Bible and Prophetic Conference was held in New York City in 1878', six more followed
Brookes (27 Feb 1830 - 18 Apr 1897), Presbyterian, Walnut Street Presbyterian Church St. Louis (1864), Washington and Compton Presbyterian from 1879; edited The Truth; largely wrote the Niagara Creed

Scofield came under Brookes's mentorship; assisted Moody's St. Louis campaign late 1879; secretary of St. Louis YMCA; attended Niagara 1888; pastor of Moody's East Northfield church 1895; presided at Moody's funeral 1899; Ryrie argues Scofield followed Isaac Watts's dispensational scheme rather than Darby's; Gaebelein among seven consulting editors, Sandeen: 'Apparently Scofield only meant to acknowledge their assistance'

Weber: Moody 'was an early convert to premillennialism', not a very doctrinaire dispensationalist; 'Almost without exception, the scores of Bible institutes founded between 1880 and 1940 taught the new premillennialism'
Moody: 'I look upon this world as a wrecked vessel. God has given me a life boat and said to me, "Moody, save all you can"'

Moody Bible Institute: Chicago Evangelization Society founded at meeting 22 January 1886, renamed after Moody's death 1899; BICA 1894 (Moody Press 1941); WMBI 1926; historically identified as dispensational and Zionist

Gaebelein born Germany 27 Aug 1861, emigrated 1879, German Methodist; Jewish mission work from 1887, full-time 1891; Tiqweth Israel 1893; Our Hope 1894 with Stroeter, editor after 1896, sympathetic to Zionism; Scofield asked him for the prophetic portions; died Christmas Day 1945

Gaebelein left the Methodist Episcopal Church in 1899; 1905: 'Zionism is not the divinely promised restoration of Israel'; 'a political and philanthropic undertaking'; 'a movement ... of unbelief'; Mouly & Robertson (1983) call his writing anti-Jewish in places; Rausch (1980) on his journal's coverage of Nazi atrocities 1937-45

ts3_audit.topic: Audit re-checks for Part Three (21 October 2026)

claims.text: Audit: the claim that Darby had written pre-tribulation views by January 1827 rests on John L. Bray (1992), cited in the MacDonald article; the Brethren sent Darby and B. W. Newton to investigate the manifestations, which they judged demonic; MacDonald's 'fiery trial which is to try us' reads as posttribulational and was omitted in 1861.
Audit: Strand reports that MacPherson cited an 1830 visit by Darby to the Macdonalds as the occasion of the alleged borrowing.
Audit: one extended Darby journey ran from Toronto to Sydney by way of San Francisco, Hawaii and New Zealand; the Darby article does not say he taught a Jewish return before Christ's return.
Audit: Scofield wrote to Gaebelein that he would 'sit at your feet when it comes to prophecy'.
